extracted.intended_audience: arts & entertainment readers interested in comedy, queer representation, and LGBTQ+ culture
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for creating and performing comedy (especially stand-up and queer-focused comedy), and for producing sensitive documentary/film work about queer subjects. Covers material selection, performance technique, representation, and production ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing / perfectly timed pause
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of pace and silence — the piece highlights Tig Notaro as an example of a performer who is a “master of the perfectly timed pause.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat pauses and pacing as a core tool for comedy delivery; timing can be a signature device that enhances jokes and emotional beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection-driven material selection
rubrics_metrics.description: “It really comes down to connection. Whether it’s a personal story or something observational, I have to feel a strong connection to it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose material because the performer feels a clear personal or thematic connection; material that resonates internally is more likely to resonate with audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test new material on stage
rubrics_metrics.description: “Other times, I test it out on stage a few times to see if it clicks.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use live performances as experiments—try bits repeatedly in front of audiences to learn whether they land and refine timing, wording, and delivery based on real reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal vs. private boundary setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide consciously “what parts of your life to bring to the stage, and what to keep private.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh vulnerability against privacy; bring personal stories that serve connection and comedic purpose, and keep private matters private when they don’t strengthen the set or could cause harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer amusement as a signal
rubrics_metrics.description: “If I’m amused or entertained by what I’m saying, chances are the audience will be too.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the performer's own amusement as an early indicator of a joke’s potential—if the comedian finds it funny, it often translates to audience engagement, but still validate via testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of funniness beyond identity
rubrics_metrics.description: On the evolution of LGBTQ+ performers: “within comedy, if you’re funny, people generally don’t care about your sexuality or gender.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for humor that connects on human terms; while identity informs voice, comedic success often depends on universality and craft rather than the performer’s sexual or gender identity alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical grounding in documentary/portrait production
rubrics_metrics.description: As a producer on Andrea Gibson’s documentary: “everything needed to be rooted in love and support for Andrea and their wife, Meg. That was my North Star… any decision I make on the film is guided by that principle: doing right by them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the well‑being, dignity, and wishes of documentary subjects; use ethical guardrails (rooting work in care/support) to guide editorial and production decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain compassionate tone / ‘compartmentalized joy’
rubrics_metrics.description: Working on a film about a dying friend was described as a “compartmentalized joy” — filled with love and laughter despite a serious subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance difficult subject matter with moments of joy and levity where appropriate; maintaining compassion and hope can create a fuller, more humane narrative without exploiting pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative process free of ego
rubrics_metrics.description: The documentary experience “didn’t have” the usual egos; collaboration stayed focused on the subject and yielded something positive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster collaborative environments where differing opinions don’t become ego battles; center the project’s mission and the people it represents rather than individual agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting and representation inclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: On Catherine McCafferty’s show: “When we are casting a season, we cast a wide net, because there are really funny people who live in all different kinds of bodies, and they should have a platform!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively seek diverse performers across body types, backgrounds, and identities; avoid tokenism by centering a broad range of voices and comedic styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform queer joy while allowing nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: McCafferty: “My primary goal with Pretty Gay [is] to really just platform queer joy… We want to have real conversations, but we also want to laugh! … [queer people] get to be dumb too — it’s not all just like crying, coming out, and not being accepted.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create work that foregrounds joyful, silly, and quotidian experiences of queer people alongside serious discussions; present full humanity rather than a single narrative of struggle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating marginalized groups as monoliths
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whenever you are part of a marginalized group, people are going to look at you as a monolith… When we are casting a season, we cast a wide net…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally show internal diversity within communities — varied bodies, experiences, and perspectives — to counter stereotyping and limited representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match aesthetics and technical approach to story
rubrics_metrics.description: Quentin Lee on filmmaking: “Every story has a different way to do it… try to find out: ‘What is this? How should I approach the aesthetics’… For Ethan Mao I wanted everything in the house to be like a Greek drama, shot in 35 millimeter film. Everything outside the house, I wanted to be digital video.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let narrative themes and character perspective drive choices about format, camera, and film vs. digital techniques; technical decisions should reinforce story meaning and emotional texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage experimentation and auteur voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Lee’s advice: “They should be making what they want to make… go out and experiment.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support creative risk-taking and individual voice rather than conforming to expectations; experimentation can produce distinctive work that better expresses the creator’s intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use audience/community impact as a measure of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Notaro: feeling meaningful when others take notice and feel impact for other families; filmmakers and performers cite audience resonance and intergenerational connection as evidence of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate work not only by craft but by the effect it has on communities — normalization, visibility, connection, and joy are valid success metrics alongside critical/audience acclaim.
